title: At the restaurant: want, need, and must
goal: Order a meal from start to paying the bill, express intention with *-moqchi*, and express need with *kerak* — two forms that cover almost every "I want to" and "I have to".
bekal: telling *Menga suv kerak* apart from *Borishim kerak*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Nima buyurtma qilmoqchisiz?
dialogs.intro: A plov restaurant in Tashkent at one in the afternoon — the busiest hour. The waiter comes over with a menu.

lines.speaker: Ofitsiant:
lines.id: Welcome! What would you like to order?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: I'd like to see the menu. What do you have today?

lines.speaker: Ofitsiant:
lines.text: Osh bor, shoʻrva bor, manti ham bor.
lines.id: There's plov, there's soup, and there's manti too.
lines.literal: plov exists, soup exists, manti also exists.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Bitta osh va bitta shoʻrva bering, iltimos.
lines.id: One plov and one soup, please.
lines.literal: one plov and one soup give, please.

lines.speaker: Ofitsiant:
lines.id: What would you like to drink?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Menga koʻk choy kerak. Muzli suv ham kerak.
lines.id: I need green tea. And iced water too.
lines.literal: me-to green tea needed. ice-with water also needed.

lines.speaker: Ofitsiant:
lines.id: OK. Should the plov have meat?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ha, lekin achchiq boʻlmasin. Men achchiq yey olmayman.
lines.id: Yes, but not spicy. I can't eat spicy food.
lines.literal: yes, but spicy let-it-not-be. I spicy eat can-not-I.

lines.speaker: Ofitsiant:
lines.id: Understood. Do you need anything else?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Yoʻq, rahmat. Hisobni ham olib kelmoqchimisiz?
lines.id: No, thank you. Will you bring the bill too?
lines.literal: no, thanks. bill-(object) also take come-want-you-?

lines.speaker: Ofitsiant:
lines.text: Ovqatdan keyin olib kelaman. Yoqimli ishtaha!
lines.id: I'll bring it after the meal. Enjoy your meal!
lines.literal: meal-from after take come-I. pleasant appetite!

notes: **Buyurtma qilmoq = to order.** One of dozens of compound verbs on the pattern *[noun] + qilmoq*. Others: *ish qilmoq* (to work), *xarid qilmoq* (to shop), *taklif qilmoq* (to invite), *hazil qilmoq* (to joke).

**Menga … kerak means "I need".** Literally "to me … is needed". Note that the subject is **the thing**, not you — the same pattern as *menga yoqadi* (I like it) in unit 16 and *boshim ogʻriyapti* (my head hurts) in unit 17.
**Boʻlsinmi? = "shall it be so?"** The third-person *-sin* form, used by waiters to offer a choice. Just answer *ha* or *boʻlmasin* (no, don't).
**Yoqimli ishtaha! = "enjoy your meal".** Literally "pleasant appetite", a calque of a Russian phrase. For a more Uzbek version: *Osh boʻlsin!* — "may it be good food".

grammars.title: -moqchi: intention, plans, wanting
body: The formula: take the dictionary form in *-moq*, add *-chi*, then the person endings from unit 1. No sound changes at all.
after: **The negative doesn't use -ma- but emas**: *bormoqchi **emasman*** (I don't intend to go). It's the only verb form in this book negated the way a noun sentence is.
Don't confuse it with the habitual form: *Ertaga boraman* = "I'm going tomorrow" (certain, scheduled). *Ertaga bormoqchiman* = "I want to go tomorrow" (an intention, not yet certain).
Its past form expresses a plan that fell through: *Bormoqchi edim* = "I was going to go". A very useful sentence for apologizing.

grammars.title: Kerak: needing a thing, or needing to do something
body: One word, two patterns. Which one you use depends on what you need: a thing, or an action.

head: Pattern
Example
Meaning
rows: You don't need money for this.

after: The second pattern is built from a **verbal noun**: stem + *-(i)sh* gives "the act of". *bor-ish* = going, *ishla-sh* = working, *kut-ish* = waiting. Attach a possessive ending and you get "my going", "your working" — then *kerak* closes it.
A more formal cousin of *kerak* is *lozim* (an Arabic word) for official writing, and *shart* ("condition") for non-negotiable obligations: *Borish shart* = "going is a must".
For "not allowed", use *mumkin emas*: *Bu yerda chekish mumkin emas* = no smoking here.

blocks.text: *Osh* is cooked in a big cauldron called a *qozon*, and in many families cooking it is men's work. There's also the custom of *nahorgi osh* — morning plov served from six o'clock to hundreds of guests as part of a wedding. If you're invited, come hungry.

⚠️ *Halol* and *harom* mean halal and haram, and almost all meat in Uzbekistan is halal by default. The thing to ask is actually *choʻchqa goʻshti bormi?* (is there pork?) at Russian or Korean restaurants, of which Tashkent has quite a few.
Ten sentences, in order from walking in to walking out.

Note the ending **-siz** in *goʻshtsiz* (without meat): it means "without", like English "-less", and its partner *-li* means "with". *Goʻshtli* (with meat), *muzli* (iced), *shakarsiz* (sugar-free), *tuzsiz* (unsalted). These two endings unlock dozens of words at once.
